☆ Methodological Assessment of Instrumented Indentation for Spatially Resolved Mesoscale Stiffness and Creep in Short Fiber-Reinforced Injection-Molded PBT Components
Eduard Klatt, Natalie Rauter
Instrumented indentation enables assessment of local mechanical properties in heterogeneous polymer systems, but specimen preparation and the selected indentation protocol significantly influence the quantitative interpretation of the measured response. This study develops and evaluates an experimental methodology for spatially resolved mesoscale characterization of both unreinforced and short fiber-reinforced composites. An unreinforced material system is used as a reference material to systematically examine the effects of indentation spacing, surface preparation, maximum indentation load, temporal loading parameters, and unloading evaluation. Indentation loads of 500, 1000, and 1750 mN are investigated in complementary experimental campaigns. The apparent indentation modulus exhibits moderate sensitivity to indentation load and loading time within the studied ranges. In contrast, indentation depth and the creep-related depth increment display greater sensitivity to the applied load history. Surface polishing minimizes topographical disturbances and enables reliable identification of residual indentation profiles and pile-up. Based on these methodological findings, a final load-hold-unload protocol with an indentation load of 1750 mN, a loading time of 6 s, a holding period of 300 s, and an unloading time of 4 s is applied to both unreinforced material and short fiber-reinforced composites. The mean apparent indentation modulus increases from 2.91 GPa for unreinforced material to 6.65 GPa for short fiber-reinforced composites, while the mean depth of indentation creep decreases from 2.36 to 1.91 microns. The coefficient of variation also increases for both quantities, indicating that short-fiber reinforcement enhances mean local stiffness and introduces pronounced spatial heterogeneity in both stiffness-related and time-dependent mesoscale indentation responses.
☆ Stabilizing Neural Emulation of Spatiotemporal Physical Dynamics through Denoising Koopman Latent Dynamics
Chenxu Wu, Sixing Chen, Junming Hou, Jiahan Huang, Jianqiao Zeng, Peiming Luo, Liang Yan, Jian Wei You
Koopman operator theory provides a principled framework for reduced-order modeling of nonlinear spatiotemporal dynamics through linear evolution in an observable space. In practice, however, learned finite-dimensional representations are typically approximately invariant, causing unresolved dynamics and accumulated closure errors. Recent approaches, inspired by the Mori-Zwanzig formalism, address these effects through deterministic memory or closure modeling, yet robust extrapolation beyond the training horizon remains challenging. Here, we propose KoopFlow, an efficient prediction-correction framework based on the key insight that finite-dimensional Koopman error accumulation can be reinterpreted as a progressive distributional degradation process. Accordingly, KoopFlow treats Koopman predictions as noisy intermediate estimates, which are then transported toward the target latent distribution through a generative model, thereby mitigating accumulated errors while retaining computational efficiency and temporal flexibility. Moreover, we reveal a non-monotonic relationship between Koopman spectral coherence and predictive accuracy. Experiments across diverse nonlinear dynamical systems demonstrate improved long-horizon prediction accuracy and stability over representative baselines, particularly beyond the training horizon.

☆ Optimized size, shape and orientation of rhombic transposition flaps and excisions by gradient-based methods
Niels Aage, Brandon Marshal Parks
This work presents a new method for gradient-based optimization of the rhombic transposition flap and the excision it closes, which set the strain of the skin after closure. Previous studies swept at most three parameters. Here, using structural optimization methods, up to eight variables, two flap angles, two cut lengths and the size, shape and position of the rhombic excision, are optimized under up to 32 geometric and stress constraints. The skin is a pre-stretched, incompressible hyperelastic membrane that wrinkles instead of carrying compression. Smoothed level-sets on a fixed grid represent the cuts, and springs between interpolated points the sutures, so designs change without remeshing and the adjoint method gives the sensitivities. The energy the surgery adds to the skin is minimized, and the model reproduces the energies of a published 48-design sweep with a median deviation of 5%. The optimal flap angles, $(-23^\circ, 31^\circ)$, lie outside the swept range and add 63% less energy than the Limberg flap and 15% less than the best swept design. Under unequal in-vivo tension, the optimal flap turns with the direction of the tension. Fitting the excision to the lesion and its margin lowers the energy by a further 35%, and with all eight variables it is 78% below the Limberg flap. This optimum is the same for finer grids, narrower cuts and wider undermining, although wider undermining reduces its gain. Lowering its suture-line stress by 41% costs only 2.3% more energy.

☆ Theory-guided relational learning for data product pricing: An interpretable meta-path-guided graph neural network approach
Ruize Gao, Feng Xiao, Jinpu Li, Ke Tang, Shaoze Cui
Data products are non-standardized and context-dependent, so their prices are jointly shaped by product attributes and contextual factors such as provider reputation, product comparability, and industry structure. We formulate data product pricing as a learning task over a heterogeneous information network spanning data products, providers, marketplaces, industries, and pricing modes, and design theory-grounded meta-paths, brand-based, similarity-based, industry-based, and hybrid, to characterize distinct pricing mechanisms. Building on this network, we propose a Meta-Path-Guided Heterogeneous Graph Neural Network (MPGNN), which learns path-specific representations, fuses them through an attention-based gate, and is further augmented with large language model-generated textual features. Empirical evaluation shows that MPGNN achieves statistically significant improvements over baseline models in both regression and classification across different pricing modes, and that provider-involving meta-paths dominate the learned weights, yielding predictive evidence consistent with a brand-equity-related pricing mechanism. The proposed framework combines predictive accuracy with theory-driven interpretability, offering a transferable methodological template for pricing other non-standardized digital assets.
☆ LLM-Generated Investment Research Memos Need Validation NeurIPS 2026
Xukang Gong, Chenri Luo, Binyan Yu, Xiao-Yang Liu
LLMs are increasingly adopted to draft long-form investment research memos, but their reliability is judged claim by claim, while readers read each memo as a whole. In this paper, we show that a low claim-level error rate does not necessarily mean that a memo is reliable: even with a refutation rate of just 1-2%, roughly four in ten memos contain at least one claim contradicted by official filings. First, we generate 1,440 memos with four recent LLM-powered agents for 30 companies over 12 quarters, decompose them into 77,272 financial claims, and verify each against the same official source bundle by retrieving evidence, matching it to the claim, and verifying the outcome. Second, we find that only 1.17-1.77% of claims are refuted, yet 36.94-41.11% of memos contain at least one refuted claim, and agents differ in severity: Codex has the lowest memo-level rate; a qualitative review further groups errors into four patterns (time, unit, context, concept).

☆ Inferring Factor Importance with Explainable AI Model for Macrophage Immune Cell Polarization
Joseph Pateras, Gurseerat Kaur, D. Joshua Cohen, Barbara D. Boyan, Zvi Schwartz, Preetam Ghosh
Macrophages are highly plastic immune cells that dynamically shift between pro- and anti-inflammatory phenotypes in response to cytokines, transcriptional regulators, metabolic cues, and local microenvironment. Yet macrophage polarization is governed by nonlinear regulatory networks that are difficult to study experimentally. Here, we integrate mechanistic simulation, surrogate neural networks, and explainable machine learning to identify key regulatory drivers of polarization. We generated simulation data with a COPASI-based macrophage polarization model and used them to train an LSTM surrogate capable of reconstructing temporal macrophage marker dynamics across diverse macrophage activation states. SHAP, Individual Conditional Expectation, and Partial Dependence Plot analyses quantified feature importance, identified nonlinear response regimes, and characterized higher-order interactions among cytokines, transcription factors, and polarization markers. The model identified oxygen availability and IL10 as dominant anti-inflammatory regulators, consistently promoting M2-associated outputs such as ARG1 and VEGF. Conversely, IFN-γ, TNFα, IL12, iNOS, CXCL9, and mCXCL10 reinforced M1-associated inflammatory programs. STAT1-centered analyses identified iNOS, TNFα, and mCXCL10 levels as strong contributors to STAT1 outcomes, consistent with amplification of the IFN- γ/JAK/STAT1 inflammatory axis. VEGF negatively contributed to predicted STAT1 output, suggesting antagonism between M2 markers and M1 activation. SHAP, ICE, and PDP analyses also showed that STAT1 regulation is nonlinear and threshold-like: pro-inflammatory signals must accumulate before STAT1 rises sharply. Together, it demonstrates that the LSTM explainability framework can identify polarization drivers, uncover nonlinear regulatory thresholds, and prioritize pathways for experimental validation.

☆ Exploring the Privacy--Size Tradeoff for Differentially Private Self-Attentive Variational Autoencoders
Rohit Sadavarte, Dhruvi Kothari, Sparsh Gupta, Eric Van Oeveren
Data tends to be most useful when it is shared, and the data most worth sharing is often the data that privacy obligations restrict. Synthetic data from a generator trained under differential privacy (DP) is one way to reconcile the two, but its utility depends on the privacy budget $\varepsilon$ and on how much data the generator sees - a parameter that most data sharing applications of synthetic data control. We present SAVANT, a self-attentive variational autoencoder for tabular data trained with DP-SGD that, to our knowledge, is the first to combine attention, a VAE, and DP in one tabular model. We evaluate it against two marginal mechanisms, PrivBayes and MST, jointly over the privacy budget and the dataset size on two public datasets, measuring the utility a downstream classifier loses by training on synthetic rather than real data. We find that, under the same DP guarantee, more data generally means more utility. For the marginal mechanisms it absorbs most of what a strict budget costs, and a noise-scaling argument suggests DP-SGD exchanges data fo budget at a worse rate. Two independent membership-inference attacks, judged against a measured null, found no aggregate membership signal.

☆ Learning Implicit Solves for Dynamic Simulations
Chawit Kaewnuratchadasorn, Jiaji Wang, Xin Nie
High-fidelity simulation of dynamical systems is central to scientific discovery and engineering design, yet remains computationally demanding. Here we introduce the Implicit Neural Operator Solver (INOS), which learns the implicit solve and encodes a time integrator. INOS pretrains a neural operator from static equilibrium solutions and reuses it within Newmark-$β$ integration. At each time increment, the integrator forms an effective equilibrium problem, the pretrained neural operator infers the next-step solution field, and the Newmark relations advance the dynamic state. Numerical examples in linear and nonlinear elastodynamics demonstrate accurate full-field predictions without dynamic trajectory supervision. Comparative results show that INOS, evaluated zero-shot, achieves higher predictive accuracy than neural solver baselines trained on dynamic simulations. In addition, INOS delivers over 4,600$\times$ speedup in nonlinear simulations over sequential classical finite-element solvers. INOS natively accommodates changes in dynamic conditions and enables reuse of the pretrained operator across spatial and temporal discretizations. Further evaluation demonstrates a stable million-step rollout. These findings establish INOS as a reusable neural implicit solver for accurate, efficient, and robust dynamic modeling.
♻ ☆ DropFENO: A Data-Free, Physics-Based Operator-Learning Framework for Droplet Equilibria on Mixed-Wettability Patterned Surfaces
Ganesh Sahadeo Meshram, Partha Pratim Chakrabarti, Suman Chakraborty
We study whether the equilibrium of a drop on a chemically patterned wall, and the capillary forces that the pattern exerts on it, can be learned from the free energy alone, without solution data. We introduce DropFENO (Droplet Free-Energy Neural Operator), in which Fourier (FNO), tensor-factorised Fourier (TFNO) and wavelet (WNO) neural operators are trained in two and three dimensions on the diffuse-interface free energy of the drop, with its volume and centroid constraints imposed as penalties. The predictions are tested with the virtual-work (Hellmann--Feynman) theorem: the force exerted by the pattern on a held drop is a wall integral of the equilibrium field which, for a drop straddling a wettability step, reduces identically to the contact-line law $F=σΔ\cosθ\,L$. DropFENO reproduces this law and the energy landscape of a drop crossing a step, and reproduces the pinning of the receding contact line less accurately. The residual error lies in the soft modes of the capillary energy (small displacements of the interface and the contact line). This explains why the energy is predicted accurately while contact-line positions are not, and why on striped walls the operators return Cassie-like states instead of the edge-pinned states whose anisotropic apparent angles the reference minimiser shares with lattice Boltzmann simulations. On held-out patterned walls the median energy of the predictions lies $\NdEmedRandFnoTwo$ of the free-drop energy above the best known minimum (FNO, two dimensions), at about one hundredth of the cost of a per-instance minimisation, and a refinement by a classical solver started from the prediction returns the reference state in almost all cases.

♻ ☆ TCBench: A Benchmark for Tropical Cyclone Track and Intensity Forecasting at the Global Scale
Milton Gomez, Marie McGraw, Saranya Ganesh S., Frederick Iat-Hin Tam, Ilia Azizi, Samuel Darmon, Monika Feldmann, Stella Bourdin, Louis Poulain--Auzéau, Suzana J. Camargo, Jonathan Lin, Dan Chavas, Chia-Ying Lee, Ritwik Gupta, Andrea Jenney, Tom Beucler
TCBench is a benchmark for evaluating global, short to medium-range (1-5 days) forecasts of tropical cyclone (TC) track and intensity. To allow a fair and model-agnostic comparison, TCBench builds on the IBTrACS observational dataset and formulates TC forecasting as predicting the time evolution of an existing tropical system conditioned on its initial position and intensity. TCBench includes state-of-the-art physics-based (TIGGE) and Artificial Intelligence Weather Prediction (AIWP) models (AIFS, Pangu-Weather, FourCastNetV2, GenCast, FNV3P2). If not readily available, TC tracks are consistently derived from model outputs using the TempestExtremes library. TCBench provides deterministic and probabilistic storm-following metrics. On 2023 test cases, AIWP models skillfully forecast TC tracks, while realistic intensity forecasts require additional steps such as post-processing or task-specific training. Designed for accessibility, TCBench helps AI practitioners tackle domain-relevant TC challenges and equips tropical meteorologists with data-driven tools and workflows to improve prediction and TC process understanding. By lowering barriers to reproducible, process-aware evaluation of extreme events, TCBench aims to democratize data-driven TC forecasting.

♻ ☆ UQ-SHRED: uncertainty quantification of shallow recurrent decoder networks for sparse sensing via engression
Mars Liyao Gao, Yuxuan Bao, Amy S. Rude, Xingyue Zhang, Xinwei Shen, J. Nathan Kutz
Reconstructing high-dimensional spatiotemporal fields from sparse sensor measurements is critical in a wide range of scientific applications. The SHallow REcurrent Decoder (SHRED) architecture is a recent state-of-the-art architecture that reconstructs high-quality spatial domain from hyper-sparse sensor measurement streams. An important limitation of SHRED is that in complex, data-scarce, high-frequency, or stochastic systems, portions of the spatiotemporal field must be modeled with valid uncertainty estimation. We introduce UQ-SHRED, a distributional learning framework for sparse sensing problems that provides uncertainty quantification through a neural network-based distributional regression called engression. UQ-SHRED models the uncertainty by learning the predictive distribution of the spatial state conditioned on the sensor history. By injecting stochastic noise into sensor inputs and training with an energy score loss, UQ-SHRED produces predictive distributions with minimal computational overhead, requiring only noise injection at the input and resampling through a single architecture without retraining or additional network structures. On complicated synthetic and real-life datasets including turbulent flow, atmospheric dynamics, neuroscience and astrophysics, UQ-SHRED provides a distributional approximation with well-calibrated confidence intervals. We further conduct ablation studies to understand how each model setting affects the quality of the UQ-SHRED performance, and its validity on uncertainty quantification over a set of different experimental setups.
♻ ☆ A Financial Brain Scan of the LLM
Hui Chen, Antoine Didisheim, Mo Pourmohammadi, Luciano Somoza, Hanqing Tian
We use sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to "brain scan" large language models, mapping internal activations to interpretable concepts and enabling targeted "steering" of specific features. We show that prompting models to adopt specific preferences activates many unintended concepts, complicating causal inference. In contrast, SAEs permit smooth, more isolated steering of target concepts. Furthermore, our scans reveal a stark disconnect between the model's internal feature contributions and its self-generated explanations, showing that these explanations are unreliable guides to its reasoning. Finally, SAEs provide a lightweight intervention for existing models, producing interpretable embeddings and allowing researchers to attenuate specific economic biases.

♻ ☆ A Comprehensive Benchmark of Computational Models for Antibody--Antigen Binding Affinity
Xinyan Zhao, Yi-Ching Tang, Victor J Cantu, Junseok Lee, Adam E Stogsdill, Ibraheem M Hamdi, Ashwin Kumar Ramesh, Zhiqiang An, Xiaoqian Jiang, Yejin Kim
Computational antibody design requires benchmarks that measure functional binding rather than similarity to natural sequences. Here we present AbBiBench, which treats the antibody--antigen complex as the evaluation unit and harmonizes 216,560 experimental measurements spanning 13 antibodies and 9 antigens. We compare 20 computational approaches without task-specific training or fine-tuning. The analyses show that global structure-conditioned inverse folding yields the strongest and most consistent affinity rankings, whereas antibody-specific fine-tuning does not consistently improve performance. Across models, rankings are more useful for prioritizing likely affinity gains than for excluding weak variants. In a subsequent case study, multi-objective evaluation of model-generated F045-092 CDR-H3 variants for H1N1 binding revealed a trade-off between predicted binding potential and evolutionary sequence plausibility; all 21 selected candidates produced H1-reactive ELISA signals. AbBiBench provides an open framework for developing and evaluating function-aware antibody design methods.
♻ ☆ Sparse stochastic digital twins can outperform exact ones
Zongren Zou, Théo Bourdais, Ricardo Baptista, Houman Owhadi
Digital twins are often built under the assumption that greater model fidelity leads to better downstream performance. We show that this is not always the case: retaining weakly dependent or auxiliary degrees of freedom can increase the dimensionality of learning and control problems enough that a sparse stochastic surrogate outperforms even an exact high-dimensional model. To identify such structure, we introduce a framework for dependence discovery directly at the level of the full conditional law. The method combines conditional generative modeling with Gaussian-process distillation and kernel mode decomposition to quantify how strongly individual variables enter the conditional distribution, including through variability, tails, multimodality, and other features invisible to the conditional mean. The resulting dependence structure can be used both to construct sparse stochastic digital twins from data and to reduce known high-dimensional models for downstream tasks. In a modified Lunar Lander problem, an eight-dimensional sparse surrogate yields better control performance than the exact 109-dimensional simulator despite lower transition fidelity. A stochastic heat-equation example shows that the framework recovers sparse structure in a 102-dimensional data-driven setting and produces a more effective surrogate than one conditioned on all candidate inputs, while economic data demonstrate its use for identifying time-varying memory structure. These results show that model fidelity and downstream utility are distinct objectives, and that dependence discovery provides a practical route to sparse stochastic digital twins.
♻ ☆ Otter Weather: Skillful and Computationally Efficient Medium-Range Weather Forecasting
Cristiana Diaconu, Jonas Scholz, Aliaksandra Shysheya, Stratis Markou, Payel Mukhopadhyay, Miles Cranmer, Richard E. Turner
State-of-the-art medium-range AI weather models can outperform traditional Numerical Weather Prediction (NWP) but require massive training budgets. This restricts usage for under-resourced groups and severely limits fast model iteration. Here we develop Otter Weather, a highly efficient spatiotemporal forecasting model designed to democratise high-performance weather prediction with AI. Evaluated on ERA5 reanalysis data at 1.5° resolution using standard WeatherBench protocols, the Otter family significantly advances the skill-compute Pareto frontier. The deterministic version outperforms the best NWP baseline by 9.6% at a 24-hour lead time while requiring fewer than 3.5 A100-days for training. It provides a 2x efficiency gain over lightweight AI models and a 100-fold reduction in compute compared to resource-intensive frontier architectures. We extend these efficiency gains into probabilistic forecasting by training via the Continuous Ranked Probability Score (CRPS). Scaling to a larger architecture, Otter-XL achieves a 9.7% CRPS improvement over the IFS ENS baseline. This yields an almost two-fold increase in predictive skill over comparable lightweight models at similar compute budgets. Otter-XL also outperforms frontier architectures like GenCast by over 2%, while using an order of magnitude less compute. Finally, Otter is applied out-of-the-box to a complex acoustic scattering PDE task where it outperforms a state-of-the-art foundation modelling approach, suggesting that the advances made here might apply across a range of scientific domains.

☆ Pixel-UMI: Learning Environment-Aware Whole-Body Manipulation from Sensorized Human Demonstrations
Jason Jingzhou Liu, Tony Tao, Deepak Pathak, Ruslan Salakhutdinov
Sensorized human demonstrations offer scalable data for mobile manipulation, but embodiment differences complicate policy learning. We present Pixel-UMI, a pipeline for learning environment-aware whole-body policies from human data. We first introduce Environment-Aware Retargeting (EAR), which combines reconstructed scene geometry with demonstrated head and gripper trajectories to determine robot posture and generate collision-aware joint and base targets. Delay-calibrated action assignment converts these trajectories into actions. However, kinematic differences can leave residual pose errors, creating viewpoint mismatches between human demonstrations and robot observations. We therefore introduce Retargeting-Error-Aware Masking (REAM), which uses these errors during training to reduce reliance on mismatched views at deployment. Finally, because estimated actions cannot fully capture contact-rich interactions, we collect on-policy human corrections through DAgger to improve performance. We evaluate Pixel-UMI on five challenging tasks spanning articulated-object manipulation, deformable-object handling, constrained-space reaching, whole-body collision avoidance, and contact-rich bimanual coordination, achieving 87.0% average task progress. Video results are available at https://pixel-robot.com/pixel-umi

☆ Pixel: A Co-Designed Full-Stack Robot System for Learning General-Purpose Mobile Manipulation
Tony Tao, Jason Jingzhou Liu, Ruslan Salakhutdinov, Deepak Pathak
General-purpose mobile manipulation requires a combination of capable robot hardware, scalable demonstration collection, expressive whole-body control, and effective policy learning. Yet these components are often developed independently, creating mismatches that limit the capabilities of the complete system. We present Pixel, a co-designed full-stack system for learning general-purpose mobile manipulation. Pixel combines a low-cost wheeled humanoid with human-aligned kinematics and compliant grippers, multiple teleoperation and robot-free human data-collection interfaces, a unified whole-body controller, and a common policy learning pipeline across human and robot demonstrations. A hierarchical learning stack further enables language-conditioned visuomotor control and long-horizon task execution. In a linear associative memory, we prove that after one update the margin-to-spread ratio of gradient descent gains on that of Muon as the data budget grows, and simulations show that this trend persists after extended training.

The results illustrate a practical accuracy-efficiency trade-off: for this exemplar, embedded training provides the strongest average accuracy, while the staged approach yields comparable qualitative behavior with a moderate increase in error, substantially fewer model evaluations, and improved optimization robustness.

We present a variational functional neural network (vfNN) algorithm that optimizes physically motivated continuum functionals in integral form (e.g., Lagrangian, Hamiltonian, or free energy) to find the states of a system. For this emergent nonconvex optimization problem, we develop a quasi-Newton optimization algorithm with simulated annealing that converges to the solutions of the corresponding Euler-Lagrange equations of the functional regardless of their stability properties. ☆ Tilted Convexity and an Exact Offline-Online Separation

Convexity has three equivalent descriptions: support by affine functions, monotonicity of the subdifferential, and increasing secant slopes. We weaken all three by one distortion with parameter $γ\in(0,1]$, which multiplies positive changes by $γ$ and divides negative ones by $γ$. The resulting classes are the convex functions at $γ=1$ and, for $γ<1$, are distinct and nested, with the parameter dropping by at most a square along the chain. For proper lower semicontinuous functions in these classes, the effective domain is convex, local minimizers are global, and the function is locally Lipschitz on the relative interior of its domain. The classes separate offline from online optimization over compact convex sets with efficient projection, with access to function values and bounded support vectors. A smooth member of any class can be minimized to additive accuracy $\varepsilon$ with $\mathrm{poly}(1/\varepsilon)$ first-order queries and projections. Online, with nonpositive losses and $α$-regret measured against $α$ times the best fixed point, a polynomial-time algorithm achieves $γ$-regret $O(\sqrt T)$ on the largest class. For every fixed, effectively specified $γ\in(0,1)$ and every $α\in(γ,1]$, no randomized polynomial-time algorithm has sublinear expected $α$-regret unless $\mathbf{NP}=\mathbf{RP}$, already for smooth concave polynomial losses in the smallest class, each minimized by one linear optimization. Thus, unless $\mathbf{NP}=\mathbf{RP}$, $γ$ is the exact online coefficient of each class, while the offline coefficient is one.

The probability of successful certification is characterized theoretically. Training on unrolled trajectories is known to limit these divergences but quickly becomes too computationally expensive due to the need to compute gradients over an iterative process, making this method impractical for large-scale physical systems (e.g. weather and climate forecasting). Two popular paradigms for improving the stability of learned dynamics are to train on interpolated or noisy samples or to regularize the Jacobian of the learned representation. In this work, we demonstrate that these paradigms can be understood under a common lens and that they both correspond to an approximation of the gradients obtained in an unrolled learning strategy. Building on this understanding, we derive a principled and complete approach to regularize training and demonstrate its impact on the stability of learned dynamical systems.

☆ Improving Hamiltonian Learning through Local Energy Decomposition

Hamiltonian neural networks provide a principled framework for learning conservative dynamics. A scalar Hamiltonian is parameterized by a neural network and the vector field is derived using Hamilton's equations. However, preserving Hamiltonian structure does not guarantee that the energy function itself is represented accurately. When modeled by a conventional multilayer perceptron, the Hamiltonian inherits the spectral bias of coordinate-based neural representations, favoring smooth over fine-scale structure. These fine-scale errors can be amplified by differentiation when computing the dynamics. To address this limitation, we introduce Local Multiscale Hamiltonian Neural Network (LM-HNN), which restructures the Hamiltonian according to its physical interaction structure. LM-HNN decomposes the energy into kinetic and potential components and represents them as sums of shared local functions over multiple interaction neighborhoods. This replaces a single high-dimensional approximation problem with lower-dimensional, reusable interaction laws, making fine-scale energy structure easier to resolve while preserving Hamiltonian dynamics. Across low-dimensional, interacting, and fast--slow systems, LM-HNN consistently achieves more accurate Hamiltonian derivatives and long-horizon rollouts than competing structure-preserving models, while substantially extending the effective spectral range of the learned energy. The same structured representation also generalizes more reliably to energy levels not observed during training. These results show that accuracy depends on the Hamiltonian representation as well as its structure, and that incorporating locality, decomposition, and shared interaction laws provides a simple and effective route to more accurate and generalizable Hamiltonian learning.

☆ Causal discovery needs explicit epistemic standards NeurIPS 2026
Harald Kugler, Leonard Henckel, Sebastian Weichwald
There are many causal discovery algorithms, but few guiding principles for choosing between them. Methods are usually compared through three lenses: identifiability, consistency, and benchmarks. Each introduces assumptions about the data-generating process that are often untestable. We argue that there are no shared standards for comparing, prioritizing, or even discussing those assumptions. We support this claim by showing that (i) identifiability assumptions are often preferred by convention rather than by principle, (ii) uniform consistency requires further untestable assumptions, while the weaker pointwise consistency has arguably narrowed algorithm design, and (iii) benchmarks are not neutral tests but carry an epistemic role of their own: they quietly fix which regimes matter, which guarantees come into play, and what counts as success. In doing so, they shape what algorithm comparisons are taken to show and thus perform some of the same epistemic work as theory, but less transparently. In this position paper we argue for a more transparent, integrated practice: Make the epistemic standards for discussing identifiability and consistency assumptions explicit, especially their failure modes and scope conditions; design benchmarks to operationalize those standards, by stress-testing and ablating both. Then, theoretical and empirical results jointly clarify when, why, and how algorithms may work rather than accumulate as disconnected advances.

It further establishes that PID is inexpensive and well codified but limited by nonlinearity, time variation, discrete mode switching, loop interaction and slow plant dynamics, while RL's admissible position must be argued rather than assumed. Conventional federated learning (FL) relies on parameter averaging, which forces clients to be doubly homogeneous: it demands an identical architecture and degrades under non-IID data. Real-world deployments usually break both assumptions. We sidestep both by building a decentralized knowledge distillation framework in which each client evaluates its peers' model snapshots on its own local data and distills from the resulting soft predictions. Because knowledge is transferred through the shared class posterior, clients are free to run different architectures; and because every teacher is evaluated on the student's own device, raw data never leaves the client, with no central server or public dataset required. Within this setting, we identify and address an under-examined problem: how to combine the peer teacher predictions. Existing methods, like uniform averaging, ignore how knowledge reliability varies across teachers and classes. We propose Class-wise Reliability-Aware Distillation (CRAD), which, per class, first discards teachers that disagree with the peer consensus and then takes a weighted average of the rest, weighting each teacher by its per-class reliability (precision, or inverse variance). Since the variance of an accuracy from $n$ samples scales as $1/n$, support enters automatically: among the teachers that survive filtering, a teacher is trusted for a class to the degree that it is both accurate and well-evidenced for it. On CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and PathMNIST, across heterogeneous architectures under severe non-IID skew, CRAD consistently outperforms competing methods in global accuracy. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/bbilbeis/CRAD.

In particular, PullbackAscent improves mean scores over GradientAscent across all five primary metrics on each architecture, reducing mean Infidelity by factors of 2.8 to 5.5. Strikingly, it also produces sharp, perceptually aligned and target-specific perturbations in only a few steps, without post-processing or explicit perceptual priors. More broadly, pullback-based methods achieve the best mean in 13 out of 15 architecture-metric combinations, outperforming established attribution baselines. Our results suggest that adjoint transport can serve as a reusable backward primitive, enhancing existing explanation procedures without architectural changes or elaborate attribution pipelines. We use "Semantic Pullbacks" (SP) to denote the resulting family of pullback-based explanations.

♻ ☆ An Agentic AI Workflow for Liver Lesion Segmentation and Structured Radiology Reporting
Fatma Ahmed Mansour, Rahatara Ferdousi, Zyad Medhat Mahmoud Ashor, Manar Fathy Elshenawy, Ibrahim Shehaby, Salma Elmongi, S. Ahmed
Despite advances in automated liver lesion segmentation, a gap remains between image-derived predictions and clinically interpretable radiology reports. Bridging this gap requires quantitative measurements that are both reproducible and traceable. We present an evidence-grounded agentic AI framework that connects liver and lesion segmentation with deterministic quantification and structured reporting. TotalSegmentator-based nnU-Net models delineate the liver, Couinaud segments, and lesions, while computational tools extract volumes, dimensions, counts, and anatomical locations. A large language model (LLM) organizes these measurements into a predefined reporting schema, with numerical consistency checks against source measurements. On 51 LiTS cases, the segmentation stage achieved a liver Dice score of 0.947, lesion sensitivity of 75.6%, and positive predictive value of 68.9%. Exploratory screening of 25,494 MERLIN reports identified 10,208 (40.0%) with liver-related abnormalities. By connecting quantitative imaging evidence with agentic report generation, this work takes a step toward human-centered medical AI that prioritizes traceability and clinical relevance.
♻ ☆ Training Agents to Fail Predictably: Fine-Tuning for Forecastable Tail Risk NeurIPS 2026
Will Schwarzer, Scott Niekum
Estimating how often an ML model will fail at deployment scale is central to pre-deployment safety assessment, but a feasible evaluation set is rarely large enough to observe the failures that matter. Jones et al. (2025) address this by extrapolating from the largest k failure scores in an evaluation set to predict deployment-scale failure rates. We give a finite-k decomposition of this estimator's forecast error and show that it has a built-in bias toward over-prediction in the typical case, which is the safety-favorable direction. This bias is offset when the evaluation set misses a rare high-failure mode that the deployment set contains, leaving the forecast to under-predict at deployment scale. We propose a fine-tuning objective, the forecastability loss, that addresses this failure mode. In two proof-of-concept experiments, a language-model password game and an RL gridworld, fine-tuning substantially reduces held-out forecast error while preserving primary-task capability and achieving safety similar to that of supervised baselines.
comment: To appear at NeurIPS 2026. 32 pages, 9 figures. Previously titled "Training ML Models with Predictable Failures"
♻ ☆ Generating Financial Time Series by Matching Random Convolutional Features
Konrad J. Mueller, Nikita Zozoulenko, Ben Wood, Thomas Cass, Lukas Gonon
Generating realistic financial time series is challenging as training data is often limited to a single historical path. With such scarce data, overfitting is hard to avoid, especially under adversarial training where a trained discriminator can memorize the training samples. To mitigate this, recent approaches train generators to minimize the discrepancy between untrained feature representations of real and generated time series. In these works, the feature maps are based on path signatures, which can fail to capture relevant time series properties at tractable truncation depths. In this work, we instead train generators by matching random convolutional features of real and generated time series. Existing random convolutional feature maps, such as Rocket and Hydra, have been shown to provide informative representations of real-world time series, but cannot supervise generative models because they are non-differentiable. We introduce SOCK (SOft Competing Kernels), a fully differentiable random convolutional feature map, suited to train generative time series models. We show that generators trained by matching random SOCK features outperform signature and diffusion baselines on most evaluation metrics across a wide range of small-sample financial datasets. We further demonstrate SOCK's expressiveness on two-sample hypothesis testing and time series classification tasks, where SOCK matches or outperforms existing unsupervised feature maps.
♻ ☆ Tune-Up Open-Weight CLIP: Optimization Framework for Self-Supervised Fine-tuning of CLIP NeurIPS 2026
Anant Mehta, Xingyu Chen, Xiyuan Wei, Tianbao Yang
CLIP has become a cornerstone of multimodal representation learning, yet improving its performance typically requires a prohibitively costly process of training from scratch on billions of samples. We ask a different question: Can we improve the performance of open-weight CLIP models across various downstream tasks using only existing self-supervised datasets? Unlike supervised fine-tuning, which adapts a pretrained model to a single downstream task, our setting seeks to improve general performance across various tasks. However, as both our experiments and prior studies reveal, simply applying standard training protocols starting from an open-weight CLIP model often fails, leading to performance degradation. In this paper, we introduce TuneCLIP, a self-supervised fine-tuning framework that overcomes the performance degradation. TuneCLIP has two key components: (1) a warm-up stage of recovering optimization statistics to reduce cold-start bias, inspired by theoretical analysis, and (2) a fine-tuning stage of optimizing a new contrastive loss to mitigate the penalization on false negative pairs. Our extensive experiments show that TuneCLIP consistently improves performance across model architectures and scales. Notably, it elevates leading open-weight models like SigLIP (ViT-B/16), achieving gains of up to +2.5% on ImageNet and related out-of-distribution benchmarks, and +1.2% on the highly competitive DataComp benchmark, setting a new strong baseline for efficient post-pretraining adaptation. The code is available at https://github.com/Optimization-AI/TuneCLIP.
comment: NeurIPS 2026 spotlight
♻ ☆ OmniGuide: Universal Spatial Guidance Fields for Enhancing Generalist Robot Policies
Yunzhou Song, Long Le, Yong-Hyun Park, Jie Wang, Junyao Shi, Lingjie Liu, Jiatao Gu, Eric Eaton, Dinesh Jayaraman, Kostas Daniilidis
Vision-language-action (VLA) models have shown great promise as generalist policies for a large range of relatively simple tasks. However, they demonstrate limited performance on more complex tasks, such as those requiring complex spatial or semantic understanding, manipulation in clutter, or precise manipulation. We propose OmniGuide, a flexible framework that improves VLA performance on such tasks by leveraging arbitrary sources of guidance, such as 3D foundation models, semantic-reasoning VLMs, and human pose models. We show how many kinds of guidance can be naturally expressed as differentiable energy functions with task-specific attractors and repellers located in 3D space, that influence the sampling of VLA actions. In this way, OmniGuide enables guidance sources with complementary task-relevant strengths to improve a VLA model's performance on challenging tasks. Extensive experiments in both simulation and real-world environments, across diverse sources of guidance, demonstrate that OmniGuide enhances the performance of state-of-the-art generalist policies (e.g., $π_{0.5}$, GR00T N1.6) significantly across success and safety rates. Critically, our unified framework matches or surpasses the performance of prior methods designed to incorporate specific sources of guidance into VLA policies. Project page: https://omniguide.github.io/

♻ ☆ Thinking in Different Spaces: Domain-Specific Latent Geometry Survives Cross-Architecture Translation
Marcus Armstrong, Navid Ayoobi, Arjun Mukherjee
We investigate whether independently trained language models converge to geometrically compatible latent representations, and whether this compatibility can be exploited to correct model behavior at inference time without any weight updates. We learn a linear projection matrix that maps activation vectors from a large teacher model into the coordinate system of a smaller student model, then intervene on the student's residual stream during generation by substituting its internal state with the translated teacher representation. Across a fully crossed experimental matrix of 20 heterogeneous teacher-student pairings spanning mixture-of-experts, dense, code-specialized, and synthetically trained architectures, the Ridge projection consistently achieves R^2 = 0.50 on verbal reasoning and R^2 = 0.40 on mathematical reasoning, collapsing to R^2 = -0.22 under permutation control and R^2 = 0.01 under L_1 regularization. Behavioral correction rates range from 14.0% to 50.0% on TruthfulQA (mean 25.2%) and from 8.5% to 43.3% on GSM8K arithmetic reasoning (mean 25.5%), demonstrating that the method generalizes across fundamentally different reasoning domains. We report a near-zero correlation between geometric alignment quality and behavioral correction rate (r = -0.07), revealing a dissociation between representation space fidelity and output space impact. Intervention strength is architecture-specific: student models exhibit characteristic sensitivity profiles that invert across domains, with the most steerable verbal student becoming the least steerable mathematical student. Finally, a double dissociation experiment conducted across all 20 model pairings confirms without exception that projection matrices collapse catastrophically when transferred across reasoning domains (mean R^2 = -3.83 in both transfer directions), establishing domain-specific subspace geometry as a universal property of LMs.

♻ ☆ The Role of Quantization in Loss Spikes
Zaiqian Chen, Aditya Somasundaram, Sophie Li, Sean McLeish, John Kirchenbauer, Tom Goldstein, Micah Goldblum
Loss spikes in language model pretraining can waste substantial compute and derail otherwise healthy training runs. A primary driver of these instabilities is the growth and divergence of output logits in the final language modeling (LM) head. In this work, we study a particularly costly form of this instability associated with output logit growth: delayed, terminal divergences that emerge only after prolonged training, which we call time-bomb spikes. We find that these instabilities are preceded by rapidly growing quantization error in the LM head, which eventually culminates in a loss spike. Crucially, reducing numerical precision accelerates time-bomb spikes, while increasing precision improves stability. We then propose a simple yet effective mitigation that replaces AdamW on the LM head with SGD with momentum, suppressing logit growth and improving stability over long training horizons. Finally, we find that existing mitigation techniques from the literature (along with our own) all reduce quantization error, suggesting a shared numerical mechanism behind their effectiveness. Together, our results identify finite precision error as a hidden driver of time-bomb spikes and show that suppressing this error is key to stable long-horizon pretraining.
♻ ☆ Causal DAG-Guided Reinforcement Learning for Long-Term Physical Activity Maintenance: Using Prior Data to Inform Future Deployment
Xueqing Liu, Young Hyun Cho, Bhanu Teja Gullapalli, Predrag Klasnja, Susan Murphy
Digital health interventions can provide scalable, personalized support for physical activity (PA), yet sustaining PA over the long-term remains difficult. Because affective experiences with PA are important for activity sustainment, we developed an online reinforcement learning (RL) system for the forthcoming ADAPT factorial trial that personalizes twice-daily activity suggestions aimed at improving affective associations with PA. This setting poses several challenges: participant-specific data are scarce relative to the candidate state space, important states and rewards are partially observed, interventions are frequent while the primary outcome is measured weekly, and activity suggestions can both improve PA-related experiences and increase intervention burden. We address these challenges using an expert-specified causal directed acyclic graph as an integrated RL design tool, guiding state construction, estimation of partially observed states, delayed credit assignment, and representation of beneficial and adverse intervention pathways. We further construct a longitudinal simulator calibrated from a prior micro-randomized trial to compare candidate RL designs under realistic state evolution, missingness, and participant heterogeneity before deployment. Together, this work illustrates how causal domain knowledge and prior trial data can make long-horizon, participant-specific RL more practical for digital health interventions targeting sustained behavior change.
♻ ☆ RogueMerge: Robust and Unified Attacks against LLM Model Merging
Jinghuai Zhang, Yetian He, Kunlin Cai, Han Zhao, Fnu Suya, Yuan Tian
Model merging composes specialized capabilities into a single LLM by aggregating task-specific LLMs sourced from unverified public platforms, exposing a critical supply-chain attack surface: Because any malicious behavior can be encoded into a task vector, and merging grants third-party vectors direct write access to model weights, an attacker-provided task vector can enable or amplify diverse downstream threats. Prior work only examines backdoor attacks against model merging for classifiers using static arithmetic heuristics, which fail to effectively achieve diverse attacks on generative LLMs for three reasons: (i) LLMs rely on autoregressive decoding, where even a minor parameter drift introduced by merging compounds across tokens and rapidly degrades the attack. (ii) Attackers have no knowledge of the victim's merging configurations, causing a static attack vector optimized in isolation to be easily diluted or neutralized. (iii) Practical threat induction must generalize to attack prompts unseen during optimization, which static vectors cannot adequately encode. In light of these gaps, we present RogueMerge, the first unified attack framework addressing all three challenges. To handle autoregressive generation, we replace static arithmetic with a joint optimization that explicitly enforces attack success after merging. To better simulate unknown merging settings, we formulate attack injection as a stochastic min-max optimization problem and solve it via meta-gradient descent. To generalize across heterogeneous attack prompts, we employ distributionally robust optimization and derive a tractable first-order Taylor approximation at LLM scale, with a provable error bound. Across four threats, six merging algorithms, and over 170 merged LLMs, RogueMerge consistently outperforms prior attacks. It also remains stable across diverse merging settings and resists standard defenses.

♻ ☆ Real-time virtual circuits for plasma shape control via neural network emulators
Alasdair Ross, George K. Holt, Kamran Pentland, Adriano Agnello, Nicola C. Amorisco, Pedro Cavestany, Aran Garrod, Timothy Nunn, Charles Vincent, Graham McArdle
Reliable position and shape control in tokamak plasmas requires accurate real-time regulation of several strongly coupled shape parameters. The control vectors that disentangle these couplings, referred to as \textit{virtual circuits} (VCs), enable independent shape parameter control for a specific Grad--Shafranov (GS) equilibrium. Numerical calculation of VCs is not currently feasible in real time, therefore VCs are usually computed prior to each experiment, using a small number of reference GS equilibria sampled along the desired scenario trajectory, with each VC used to control the plasma within a preset time interval. While effective near the reference equilibrium, this approach can lead to degraded performance as the plasma departs from the reference equilibrium and/or from the desired trajectory, and it complicates the design of robust control strategies for rapidly evolving plasma configurations. In this paper, we construct neural-network-based emulators of plasma shape parameters from which VCs can be derived, to provide the MAST Upgrade (MAST-U) plasma control system with state-aware VCs in real-time. To do this, we develop an extensive library of over a million simulated GS equilibria, covering a substantial portion of the MAST-U operational space. These emulators provide differentiable functions whose gradients can be rapidly computed, enabling the derivation of accurate VCs for real-time shape control. We perform extensive verification of the emulated VCs by testing whether they disentangle the control problem. The neural-network-based approach delivers high accuracy and orthogonality across a diverse range of equilibria. This work establishes the physical validity of emulated VCs as a scalable and general alternative to schedules of precomputed VCs.

♻ ☆ Dynamic estimation of slowly varying sequences
Prashant Gokhale, Mikhail Khodak, Sandeep Silwal
We consider the problem of sequentially approximating a target function of each element in a slowly-varying sequence, i.e. one where the magnitude $α_i$ of the difference between the elements at positions $i$ and $i-1$, measured in an appropriate norm, is small. Recent work on implicit trace estimation shows that when $α_i$ is small in Frobenius norm, reusing queries to past sequence elements can reduce the overall cost. We introduce a framework that generalizes this approach to linear and nonlinear functions on normed vector spaces, obtaining sequential estimation results for matrix powers, spectral densities, Monte Carlo integration, and certain boundary value problems from partial differential equations~(PDEs). Furthermore, we develop an algorithm that locally scales the estimation budget with $α_i$, obtaining sharper path-length-style variation bounds of the form $\mathcal{O}\left(\tfrac1{ε^2}\sum_{i=1}^m α_i\right)$ on the cost of estimating a sequence of length $m$ to accuracy $ε$. This improves upon the earlier implicit trace estimation dependence on $\tfrac m{ε^2}\max_iα_i$, which results from fixing the query budget using the worst-case step size $α_i$ and is thus inefficient for stable sequences with rare bursts. Furthermore, while prior theoretical guarantees assume a known bound on the step sizes, we show in certain cases how to estimate them on the fly with (nearly) no added cost. Lastly, we complement our theoretical results with experiments demonstrating improved accuracy-cost trade-offs over prior baselines on trace estimation and Hessian tracking. In summary, our framework makes sequential approximation general-purpose and adaptive while sharpening state-of-the-art guarantees for dynamic trace estimation.
comment: Preprint. 14 pages, 4 figures
♻ ☆ Revisiting RAG Retrievers: An Information Theoretic Benchmark
Wenqing Zheng, Dmitri Kalaev, Noah Fatsi, Daniel Barcklow, Owen Reinert, Igor Melnyk, Senthil Kumar, C. Bayan Bruss
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems rely critically on the retriever module to surface relevant context for large language models. Although numerous retrievers have recently been proposed, each built on different ranking principles such as lexical matching, dense embeddings, or graph citations, there remains a lack of systematic understanding of how these mechanisms differ and overlap. Existing benchmarks primarily compare entire RAG pipelines or rely on aggregate ranking metrics (Recall, MRR, nDCG) that assume item-level independence, providing little guidance on redundancy or complementarity between retrievers. This work presents MIGRASCOPE, a Mutual Information based RAG Retriever Analysis Scope. We introduce principled metrics grounded in information theory to quantify retrieval quality, redundancy/synergy, and marginal contribution. Although the framework is designed to be applicable to any setting where a ground-truth answer can construct a pseudo chunk distribution, the present empirical study focuses on multi-hop question answering - a demanding setting where retriever complementarity is especially pronounced. On four corpora and thirteen SOTA retrievers spanning lexical, dense, and graph-based families, we show that (i) the MI-based divergence metric captures retriever quality dimensions not reflected by Recall or MRR, (ii) graph-based retrievers are redundant with each other while BM25 remains informationally complementary, and (iii) in the multi-hop QA setting, a carefully chosen ensemble guided by MI-based attribution can outperform any single retriever. We position these findings as task-specific insights and provide a reusable framework for retriever analysis that practitioners can re-estimate on their own target domains.
♻ ☆ Lower Bounds for Parallel Diffusion Sampling
Yiwen Kou, Yimeng Wang
Standard diffusion samplers generate samples through sequential evaluations of a learned score function, with each query depending on previous answers. Parallel samplers seek to accelerate this process by making multiple score queries simultaneously. We ask how many adaptive rounds are necessary when each round allows polynomially many queries. We establish the first polynomial lower bounds on the round complexity of diffusion sampling with approximate scores satisfying a mean-square accuracy guarantee. Specifically, we prove (1) a $\widetildeΩ(d^{1/3})$-round lower bound for sampling smooth, near-isotropic Gaussian mixtures in $\mathbb{R}^d$, and (2) a tight $Ω(d)$-round lower bound for uniform sampling from anisotropic axis-aligned boxes contained in the unit ball. Both bounds hold for arbitrary randomized algorithms making polynomially many queries per round at arbitrary locations and noise levels, with inverse-polynomial score error and constant total variation accuracy. Our near-isotropic construction follows the blockwise approach of earlier lower bounds for parallel matroid search and discrete sampling \cite{KUW85,AGR24}. We use independent coordinate blocks containing random codebooks with well-separated rates and construct approximate score oracles whose responses in each block depend on consistency tests in earlier blocks. Together, the rate separation and these tests ensure that each round reveals information about at most one additional block with high probability.
♻ ☆ A Study of ASR Adaptation and Representation Dimensionality Reduction in Persian Speech Emotion Recognition Using Whisper
Ali Shendabadi, Parnia Izadirad, Mostafa Salehi
Speech Emotion Recognition (SER) in low-resource languages remains a challenging problem due to limited labeled data. In this work, we study the use of Whisper for Persian SER with a particular focus on representation dimensionality reduction and language-specific model adaptation. We propose a SER framework in which frame-level embeddings extracted from the Whisper encoder are reduced in dimensionality using PCA, eliminating the need for learned projection layers and substantially reducing the number of trainable parameters. The reduced representations are aggregated using an attention-based pooling mechanism and classified with a lightweight prediction head. In addition, we investigate whether fine-tuning Whisper on a Persian automatic speech recognition (ASR) task improves downstream SER performance. Experiments conducted on the ShEMO dataset under a speaker-independent evaluation protocol show that PCA-based dimensionality reduction consistently improves emotion recognition performance while reducing training latency and memory usage. ASR fine-tuning yields only modest gains for SER, suggesting limited transfer from language adaptation to emotion-related representations under the evaluated conditions. These findings provide practical insights into the efficient use of large pretrained speech models for emotion recognition in low-resource languages.
♻ ☆ Testable and Actionable Calibration for Full Swap Regret NeurIPS 2026
Konstantina Bairaktari, Lunjia Hu, Huy L. Nguyen, Jonathan Ullman
AI generated predictions increasingly inform decision making in critical tasks, and therefore must be trustworthy. One widely used measure of trustworthiness is calibration, which requires that the predictions match the true frequencies and can be treated like real probabilities of a given outcome. However, defining calibration is subtle, and designing good measures of calibration error has been an active topic of recent research. The first goal is to find calibration measures that are actionable, meaning they can inform decision makers about their utility loss when predictions are treated as true probabilities, which is known as swap regret. The second goal is to find calibration measures that are testable, meaning that calibration error can be measured from a small sample of predictions and outcomes. Although these are very basic requirements, there is no existing calibration measure that fully satisfies both properties, and all existing measures relax actionability by bounding a weaker notion of swap regret, or relax testability by having suboptimal estimation error. We introduce a new calibration measure, Soft-Binned Calibration Decision Loss (SCDL), which we prove is fully actionable without weakening either requirement, and testable with nearly optimal error rate. In addition, SCDL satisfies other desired properties such as continuity and consistency. We also provide a set of experiments confirming that the theoretical advantages of SCDL compared to other measures lead to better performance in practice.
comment: Selected for Oral Presentation at NeurIPS 2026
♻ ☆ LNML-based Causal Discovery with Latent Confounders: Theory and Experiments ECML
Zhongyi Que, Shin Matsushima, Kenji Yamanishi
Causal discovery with nonlinear mechanisms and latent confounders remains challenging. Existing methods often rely on either linear assumptions or causal sufficiency, limiting their applicability. We propose an MDL-based causal discovery framework that accommodates latent confounders and flexible nonlinear mechanisms using the luckiness normalized maximum likelihood (LNML) code-length. To complement code-length-based model selection, we introduce $Δ$-pseudo-collinearity as a criterion for identifying potential latent-confounding candidates. We theoretically show that, in the presence of a latent confounder, the directional code-length gap $Δ$ admits an upper bound that grows at most linearly with the sample size and decreases as the latent causal mechanisms become more similar, providing support for the proposed criterion. Based on this formulation, we develop a greedy algorithm, termed Pseudo-Collinearity Guided Causal Discovery (PCG-CD). Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the ability of PCG-CD to recover directed causal relationships and identify potential latent-confounding candidates, while revealing limitations in latent-confounder discrimination.
comment: Extended version of the ECML PKDD 2026 paper titled "MDL Meets Latent Confounders: LNML-Based Causal Discovery," with additional theoretical results and experiments. The experimental implementation has been corrected, and the results have been updated accordingly
♻ ☆ Storage and Learning phase transitions in the Random-Features Hopfield Model
Matteo Negri, Clarissa Lauditi, Gabriele Perugini, Carlo Lucibello, Enrico M. Malatesta
The Hopfield model is a paradigmatic model of neural networks that has been analyzed for many decades in the statistical physics, neuroscience, and machine learning communities. Inspired by the manifold hypothesis in machine learning, we propose and investigate a generalization of the standard setting that we name Random-Features Hopfield Model. Here $P$ binary patterns of length $N$ are generated by applying to Gaussian vectors sampled in a latent space of dimension $D$ a random projection followed by a non-linearity. Using the replica method from statistical physics, we derive the phase diagram of the model in the limit $P,N,D\to\infty$ with fixed ratios $α=P/N$ and $α_D=D/N$. Besides the usual retrieval phase, where the patterns can be dynamically recovered from some initial corruption, we uncover a new phase where the features characterizing the projection can be recovered instead. We call this phenomena the learning phase transition, as the features are not explicitly given to the model but rather are inferred from the patterns in an unsupervised fashion.

♻ ☆ On the Structure of Stationary Solutions to McKean-Vlasov Equations with Applications to Noisy Transformers
Krishnakumar Balasubramanian, Sayan Banerjee, Philippe Rigollet
We study stationary solutions of McKean-Vlasov equations on the circle. We establish an exact equivalence between solutions of the stationary McKean-Vlasov equation and an infinite-dimensional quadratic system of equations over Fourier coefficients, allowing explicit characterization of stationary states in a sequence space rather than a function space. This framework provides a transparent description of local bifurcations, their periodicity and resonance structures, while accommodating singular potentials. We derive analytic expressions for the emergence, form and shape (supercritical, critical, subcritical or transcritical) of bifurcations involving possibly multiple Fourier modes and connect them with discontinuous phase transitions. We also characterize, under suitable assumptions, the detailed structure of the stationary bifurcating solutions through leading small-amplitude coefficients for arbitrarily many fixed Fourier modes. At the global level, we establish regularity and concavity properties of the free energy landscape, proving existence, compactness, and coexistence of globally minimizing stationary measures, and identifying discontinuous phase transitions with points of non-differentiability of the minimum free energy map. We apply the theory to the Noisy Mean-Field Transformer model, where we show how changing the inverse temperature $β$ affects the geometry of the infinitely many bifurcations from the uniform measure. We also discuss how increasing $β$ motivates the study of approximate multi-mode stationary profiles as candidates for a separate metastability analysis; persistence times require additional dynamical estimates. Moreover, we determine the exact threshold $β_0\simeq2.447$ separating continuous and discontinuous phase transitions in this model. The same threshold marks the change of the first bifurcation from supercritical to subcritical.

♻ ☆ Benchmarking Generalist and Specialist Time-Series Foundation Models for PPG-Based Health Assessment
Saurabh Kataria, Yi Wu, Zhaoliang Chen, Hyunjung Gloria Kwak, Yuhao Xu, Lovely Yeswanth Panchumarthi, Ran Xiao, Jiaying Lu, Ayca Ermis, Anni Zhao, Runze Yan, Minxiao Wang, Alex Fedorov, Zewen Liu, Xu Wu, Hongyu Wu, Wei Jin, Carl Yang, Jocelyn Grunwell, Stephanie R. Brown, Amit Shah, Craig Jabaley, Tim Buchman, Sivasubramanium V Bhavani, Randall J. Lee, Xiao Hu
Time-series Foundation Models (FMs) are pretrained on either heterogeneous corpora or specific signal domains. Using Photoplethysmography (PPG) as a representative modality, we compare generalist time-series FMs, PPG-specialist FMs, and traditional machine learning (ML) baselines for PPG-based health assessment. We conduct a two-stage benchmark. First, we evaluate multiple FM families across 23 downstream evaluations (e.g., atrial fibrillation detection, vital-sign estimation). Second, we conduct a focused four-FM comparison (MOMENT, Chronos-2, GPT-PPG, MOMENT-PPG) at multiple model sizes on an expanded 51-task suite, under both frozen-backbone and full-model tuning, to study tuning strategy, model scaling, and cross-dataset transfer. The multi-model benchmark shows that PPG-specialist FMs achieve the strongest aggregate performance, but their advantage is not uniform: generalist FMs remain competitive on several tasks, and traditional ML baselines outperform FMs on selected clinical regression tasks. The focused analysis shows that the advantage of PPG-specific pretraining appears mainly with frozen backbones and on targets that the waveform directly reflects, such as atrial fibrillation and vital signs. Full-model tuning narrows this advantage, model rankings change with the tuning strategy, and the largest model variant is the best choice in only about one-third of cases. Additionally, controlled experiments with two generalist models show that initializing PPG pretraining from generalist checkpoints provides an early advantage over training from scratch, even when the pretrained features offer little downstream benefit. Together, these findings suggest that PPG-specific pretraining is useful but task-dependent, and that FMs should be evaluated against simpler statistical, traditional ML, and clinical history-based baselines.
♻ ☆ Walma: Learning to See Memory Corruption in WebAssembly
Oussama Draissi, Mark Günzel, Ahmad-Reza Sadeghi, Lucas Davi
The monolithic linear memory of WebAssembly (Wasm) creates a bidirectional attack surface: a memory corruption bug in a module can compromise the host, and a compromised host can corrupt the state of a trusted module. Existing defenses either require custom runtimes or source code changes, and none can verify runtime integrity under an adversarial host. We present WALMA, the first attestation framework delivering resilience by reaction against data-centric attacks that corrupt a region of memory. We render linear memory snapshots as grayscale images and classify them with a convolutional neural network. The network reads the row-aligned structure that compiled code imposes on memory and detects corruption that byte and texture statistics miss. Our main VGG-16 detector reaches 95%--100% verdict accuracy on four of five CVE-affected applications without a single false alarm, and a 1.9M-parameter ResNet, small enough to run inside the runtime on every host call, stays within a few points of it on the same four. A Shannon-entropy analysis bounds which out-of-band edits the network can separate from valid state, and black-box evasion requires contiguous overwrites of hundreds of kilobytes to megabytes. On the 53 WABench binaries, boundary attestation costs 1.07x--1.69x, scaling with a module's exposure to the host rather than with its runtime. WALMA thus makes linear memory integrity a property a Wasm runtime can check continuously: end to end against compromised modules, and against untrusted hosts provided snapshots reach the verifier intact.

♻ ☆ A Survey of Freshness-Aware Wireless Networking with Reinforcement Learning
Alimu Alibotaiken, Suyang Wang, Oluwaseun T. Ajayi, Mushu Li, Yu Cheng
The age of information (AoI) has become a central measure of data freshness in modern wireless systems. Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a promising approach to AoI optimization, enabling adaptive decision-making in dynamic and stochastic wireless environments without requiring precise system models. Yet existing surveys either focus on classical AoI formulations or provide broad discussions of RL in wireless networks without addressing freshness as a unified learning problem. Motivated by this gap, this survey examines RL specifically through the lens of AoI and generalized freshness optimization. Motivated by this gap, this survey examines RL specifically through the lens of AoI and generalized freshness optimization. We organize AoI and its variants into native, function-based, and application-oriented families, providing a clearer view of how freshness should be modeled in B5G and 6G systems. Building on this foundation, we introduce a policy-centric taxonomy that reflects the decisions most relevant to freshness, consisting of update-control RL, medium-access RL, risk-sensitive RL, and multi-agent RL. This structure provides a coherent framework for understanding how learning can support important wireless networking problems, including sampling, scheduling, UAV trajectory planning, medium access, and distributed coordination. We further synthesize recent progress in RL-driven freshness control and highlight open challenges. The goal is to establish a unified foundation for learning-based freshness optimization in next-generation wireless networks.

♻ ☆ Inference-Time Alignment for Diffusion Models via Variationally Stable Doob's Matching
Jinyuan Chang, Chenguang Duan, Yuling Jiao, Ruoxuan Li, Yi Xu, Jerry Zhijian Yang
Inference-time alignment for diffusion models aims to adapt a pre-trained reference diffusion model toward a target distribution without retraining the reference score network, thereby preserving the generative capacity of the reference model while enforcing desired properties at inference time. A central mechanism for achieving such alignment is guidance, which modifies the sampling dynamics through an additional drift term. In this work, we introduce variationally stable Doob's matching, a novel framework for provable guidance estimation grounded in Doob's $h$-transform. Our approach formulates guidance as the gradient of the logarithm of an underlying Doob's $h$-function and employs gradient-regularized regression to simultaneously estimate both the $h$-function and its gradient, resulting in a consistent estimator of the guidance. Theoretically, we establish non-asymptotic convergence rates for the estimated guidance. Moreover, we analyze the resulting controllable diffusion processes and prove non-asymptotic convergence guarantees for the generated distributions in the Wasserstein-2 distance. Finally, we show that variationally stable guidance estimators are adaptive to unknown low dimensionality, effectively mitigating the curse of dimensionality under low-dimensional linear subspace assumptions. Numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method and show the advantages compared to the baselines.
♻ ☆ Classical State Preparation for Variational Quantum Algorithms via Reinforcement Learning
Gino Kwun, Dhanvi Bharadwaj, Gokul Subramanian Ravi
Variational Quantum Algorithms (VQAs) potentially offer a pathway to practical quantum advantage, but their optimization is heavily hindered by barren plateaus and numerous local minima. While classically simulable Clifford circuits can warm-start VQAs to accelerate convergence, existing heuristic-based initialization methods struggle to scale within vast combinatorial search spaces. We address this bottleneck with CRiSP (a Clifford Reinforcement Learning agent for State Preparation), which casts Clifford prefix selection as a sequential decision-making problem. CRiSP utilizes Neural-Guided Monte Carlo Tree Search, driven by a Transformer-based policy trained via self-play, to insert learned Clifford gates before fixed parameterized rotations. This enables the construction of high-quality initial states entirely through polynomial-time classical stabilizer simulation. By integrating a curriculum learning strategy that progressively expands the search horizon, the agent efficiently scales to deep circuits. Evaluated on QAOA benchmarks of up to $22$ qubits and $1{,}370$ parameters, CRiSP outperforms state-of-the-art Clifford initialization methods by a mean of $3.19\times$ (max $45.02\times$) in average energy accuracy and $2.41\times$ (max $16.01\times$) in best-achieved energy accuracy. Assessments on VQE tasks further demonstrate the framework's robustness and generalizability.

♻ ☆ G-NAC: Graph Neural Automata Clustering via Emergent Domain Formation
Keith Miller, Tristan Crawford, Ronald J. Stanley
We introduce Graph Neural Automata Clustering (G-NAC), an unsupervised clustering method in which observations interact as cells on a fixed neighborhood graph. A shared recurrent graph-neural cellular rule evolves latent domain states through local interactions, which are converted into a rank-based spectral affinity for partitioning. Across 73 clustering tasks from 57 benchmark datasets, G-NAC achieved a mean adjusted Rand index (ARI) of 0.7951, comparable to Genie at 0.7941 and higher than the other evaluated baselines. Empirical training time and GPU memory scaled approximately linearly from 5,000 to 100,000 nodes. Learned transition rules also transferred from smaller source graphs to independent 100,000-node samples generated under matched conditions. These results demonstrate a recurrent graph-clustering formulation while identifying dependencies on graph quality, readout design, and source-target similarity.

♻ ☆ When Human Corrections Travel: Safety in Federated VLA Adaptation SP
Vigneshwaran Subbaraju, Obaidullah Zaland, Monowar Bhuyan
Vision-language-action (VLA) policies can adapt to local human intervention, while federated learning can combine distributed robot experience without pooling raw records. We examine their prospective intersection: sharing adaptations derived from diverse human corrections across tasks, environments, people, and robot embodiments. Corrections differ in modality, safety semantics(urgency, behavioral scope, etc.), and privacy sensitivity. A shared update that improves mean task success may suppress a rare safety intervention or produce an unsafe response on another robot. We argue for three requirements: preserve the context and uncertainty of multimodal corrections when deciding what to share; assess candidate updates in each receiving robot's closed loop before deployment; and evaluate leakage alongside retention of safety-critical evidence. Immediate, legible defensive behavior remains necessary during human interaction. We offer counterexamples and a falsifiable evaluation agenda, not experimental results.
